name.text: 01 Content: The Problem IIIF Was Built to Solve

questiontext.text:
The Problem IIIF Was Built to Solve

Before 2011, a scholar wanting to compare two manuscripts held in different libraries faced a problem that had nothing to do with scholarship. Each institution had digitized its holdings, and each had built its own viewer, its own zoom mechanism, its own URL scheme, and its own download policy. The images existed. They could not be brought together.

The situation is worth naming precisely, because the diagnosis determined the cure. The failure was not a shortage of digitization — millions of folios had been scanned. It was that each digitization project produced a silo: a self-contained system whose images could be viewed only through the interface its own institution had built. Comparing a Vatican folio with a British Library folio meant opening two browser windows running two incompatible viewers, each with its own controls, neither able to display the other's images.

The workaround was worse than the problem. Scholars downloaded enormous TIFF files — gigabytes per manuscript — to compare them locally in image software. This defeated most of the purpose of digitization: it reintroduced the bottleneck of physical access in the form of bandwidth and storage, it produced uncontrolled copies detached from their metadata, and it put the burden of assembling a comparison entirely on the individual scholar (Griffin, 2023).

The International Image Interoperability Framework was designed to make the image itself a networked, addressable resource rather than a file to be transferred. Its central move is to standardize how images are requested, so that any compliant viewer can display images from any compliant server.

Vocabulary. Silo — a system whose data can be accessed only through its own interface. Interoperability — the capacity of independently built systems to work together without prior coordination.

Takeaway: IIIF exists because digitization without shared standards produced millions of images that could not be brought together.

name.text: 02 Content: Interoperability as a Scholarly Requirement

questiontext.text:
Interoperability as a Scholarly Requirement

It would be easy to read the previous page as a technical convenience argument. It is not. The inability to juxtapose witnesses is a methodological obstacle, because juxtaposition is what textual criticism does.

Collation — the operation at the centre of this course, which you will perform in Week 7 — means placing witnesses side by side and recording where they differ. For most of the discipline's history this required physical co-presence: the manuscripts in one room, or an editor travelling between libraries with notes. The great critical editions of the nineteenth century were built on exactly that labour, and their limitations reflect it.

Digitization promised to remove the constraint, and initially did not. An image locked in an institutional viewer is available for reading but not for juxtaposition, which means it supports consultation but not collation. The scholar can look at it; they cannot work with it alongside anything else.

Codex Sinaiticus is the illustrative case. The manuscript is physically divided across four institutions on three continents — the British Library, Leipzig University Library, St Catherine's Monastery, and the National Library of Russia — as a result of its nineteenth-century dispersal. Studying it as one object formerly required either extensive travel or reliance on facsimiles. Interoperable digital frameworks permit the virtual reunification of the dispersed leaves, so that an integrated palaeographical analysis becomes possible without the physical object ever being reassembled.

That is the claim worth holding onto: interoperability does not merely make existing work more convenient, it makes some scholarly operations possible for the first time.

Takeaway: Juxtaposing witnesses is the basic operation of textual criticism, and image silos prevented it — so interoperability is a methodological requirement, not a convenience.

name.text: 03 Content: Two APIs, Two Different Jobs

questiontext.text:
Two APIs, Two Different Jobs

IIIF is not one specification but a family of them. Two are foundational, and distinguishing their responsibilities is the key to understanding the whole framework.

The Image API governs the delivery of a single image. It defines a URL syntax by which a client requests a specific region of an image, at a specific size, rotation, quality, and format, and receives exactly that (Griffin, 2023). It knows nothing about books, pages, or order — its entire concern is: given this image, return this part of it, thus transformed.

The Presentation API governs structure and meaning. It describes how images assemble into an intellectual object — which images constitute a manuscript, in what order, with what labels, carrying what metadata (IIIF Consortium, 2020). It knows nothing about pixels; it refers to images by their Image API endpoints and concerns itself with arrangement and description.

Concern Image API Presentation API
Answers "Give me this part of this image" "What is this object and how is it arranged?"
Format An image (JPEG, PNG, TIFF) JSON-LD
Knows about Regions, sizes, rotation, quality Manifests, canvases, ranges, metadata
Does not know about Which manuscript this is Pixels
Delivers Image bytes A description referring to Image API endpoints

The separation is the design's central virtue. Because the two are independent, a Presentation API manifest can reference images served by any compliant Image API server anywhere in the world. A single manifest can assemble folios from the Vatican, Leipzig, and Paris into one virtual codex — which is exactly the Sinaiticus problem solved.

Takeaway: The Image API delivers pixels and the Presentation API describes structure, and their independence is what lets one manifest gather images from many institutions.

name.text: 04 Content: The Image API URL Syntax

questiontext.text:
The Image API URL Syntax

The Image API's power comes from a single well-designed URL template. Every compliant server accepts requests in the same form:

{scheme}://{server}/{prefix}/{identifier}/{region}/{size}/{rotation}/{quality}.{format}

Each segment is a parameter, and reading a IIIF URL means reading off what was requested:

Segment Meaning Example values
identifier Which image Vat.gr.1209_0042
region Which part of it full, square, 125,15,200,300, pct:10,10,50,50
size How large to return it max, 1000,, ,500, pct:50, !400,400
rotation Degrees clockwise; ! mirrors 0, 90, !180
quality Colour treatment default, color, gray, bitonal
format File format jpg, png, tif, webp

A concrete request:

https://digi.vatlib.it/iiif/MSS_Vat.gr.1209/full/1000,/0/default.jpg

This asks for the whole image, scaled to 1000 pixels wide, unrotated, in default colour, as JPEG. Changing full to 1200,400,800,600 returns only that rectangle — an 800×600 region whose top-left corner is at pixel (1200, 400).

Learn to read and write these by hand. It looks like a minor skill and is not: once you can construct an Image API URL, you can extract any region of any folio in any IIIF-compliant collection in the world, at any resolution, with a line of text. In Week 12, when your commentary needs to reproduce the exact patch of parchment supporting a disputed reading, this is how you will obtain it.

Takeaway: One URL template gives you any region of any image in any IIIF collection, at any size — learn to write it by hand.

name.text: 05 Content: Tiling and Deep Zoom

questiontext.text:
Tiling and Deep Zoom

The Image API's region-and-size parameters exist to support a specific behaviour: deep zoom, the ability to navigate a very large image smoothly without downloading it.

A high-resolution manuscript scan may be 10,000 by 14,000 pixels — around 140 megapixels, and hundreds of megabytes uncompressed. Transferring that to display a page on a screen 1,500 pixels wide is absurd: the overwhelming majority of the data cannot be displayed and is discarded on arrival.

Tiling inverts the arrangement. The server maintains the image at several resolution levels, each divided into small square tiles, typically 256 or 512 pixels on a side. When a viewer displays the whole folio, it requests a handful of tiles from a low-resolution level — enough to fill the screen at that scale. When the user zooms into a word, it requests only the few tiles at the highest resolution level that intersect the current viewport (Griffin, 2023).

View Level requested Tiles fetched Approximate data
Whole folio Lowest 4–12 A few hundred kilobytes
Half page Middle 8–20 Under a megabyte
One line, zoomed Highest 6–15 Around a megabyte
Whole folio at full resolution Highest Over 2,000 Hundreds of megabytes

The last row is the one nobody ever requests, because there is no screen on which it could be displayed. That is the insight: at any moment the user can only see one screenful, so only one screenful ever needs to be transferred, regardless of how large the underlying image is.

The practical consequence for you is that resolution is no longer something to economize. You should seek the highest-resolution IIIF source available for your passage, because the cost of high resolution is borne by the server's storage rather than by your bandwidth.

Takeaway: Tiling means only the visible screenful is ever transferred, so image resolution costs the viewer nothing.

name.text: 06 Content: The Manifest: A Digital Object's Description

questiontext.text:
The Manifest: A Digital Object's Description

Where the Image API handles pixels, the Presentation API's central document is the Manifest — a JSON-LD file describing one intellectual object, such as a manuscript, and everything a viewer needs to present it (IIIF Consortium, 2020).

A manifest states what the object is, what it is called, what metadata describes it, what rights govern it, and — centrally — what sequence of canvases constitutes it. It is the digital equivalent of a catalogue record fused with a table of contents and a set of pointers to the images themselves.

A minimal manifest, reduced to its skeleton:

{
  "@context": "http://iiif.io/api/presentation/3/context.json",
  "id": "https://example.edu/iiif/vat-gr-1209/manifest.json",
  "type": "Manifest",
  "label": { "en": ["Vaticanus graecus 1209, ff. 42r-43v"] },
  "summary": { "en": ["Fourth-century majuscule; selected folios"] },
  "rights": "http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/",
  "requiredStatement": {
    "label": { "en": ["Attribution"] },
    "value": { "en": ["Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana"] }
  },
  "items": [ ]
}

Three details are worth noticing now. The id is an HTTP URI at which the manifest itself can be retrieved — manifests are web resources, not local files, and that is what makes them shareable. Labels are objects keyed by language code holding arrays of strings, which accommodates multilingual and multi-valued descriptions natively. And rights and requiredStatement carry licensing and attribution as structured data, so that a viewer can display the required credit automatically wherever the manifest travels.

The items array — empty above — holds the canvases. That is the next section.

Vocabulary. Manifest — the JSON-LD document describing one digital object. JSON-LD — JSON with a @context mapping its keys to shared vocabulary URIs, so the data is machine-interpretable rather than merely machine-readable.

Takeaway: A manifest is a retrievable web document describing one object — its identity, metadata, rights, and the sequence of canvases that compose it.

name.text: 07 Content: The Canvas: An Abstract Space, Not an Image

questiontext.text:
The Canvas: An Abstract Space, Not an Image

The Canvas is the Presentation API's most important abstraction and the one most often misunderstood. A canvas is not an image. It is an abstract rectangular coordinate space, with a width and a height, onto which content is painted (IIIF Consortium, 2020).

The distinction sounds scholastic and is in fact the source of the model's whole expressive power. If a canvas were an image, then a page would have exactly one image, and everything this week and next depends on would be impossible. Because a canvas is a coordinate space, several things follow:

  • Multiple images can be painted onto the same canvas — a natural-light photograph, an ultraviolet capture, and a processed composite, all sharing one coordinate system.
  • Images can be painted onto part of a canvas, so that fragments recovered separately can be positioned within a reconstructed whole.
  • Non-image content can be attached — transcriptions, translations, and annotations, targeted at coordinates.
  • A canvas can exist with no image at all, representing a lost folio whose absence is part of the object's structure.

The canvas is therefore best understood as standing for the page as an intellectual entity, while images are evidence about that page. A folio photographed under five lighting conditions is one page with five pieces of photographic evidence, and the model represents exactly that: one canvas, five images.

This is the conceptual foundation for everything in Lesson 3.2, where a single folio acquires visible-light, ultraviolet, infrared, and statistically processed representations — and for Lesson 3.3, where your TEI transcription is bound to canvas coordinates rather than to any particular photograph of the page.

Takeaway: A canvas is an abstract coordinate space standing for the page itself, and images are evidence painted onto it — which is why one page can carry many images.

name.text: 08 Content: Annotations and the Painting Model

questiontext.text:
Annotations and the Painting Model

If images are not properties of a canvas, how do they attach to it? Through annotation. In Presentation API 3.0, an image is associated with a canvas by an Annotation whose motivation is painting — a statement that this image should be rendered onto that coordinate space (IIIF Consortium, 2020).

The structure nests as follows: a Canvas contains an items array holding AnnotationPages; each AnnotationPage contains an items array holding Annotations; each Annotation has a body (the content) and a target (what it applies to).

{
  "id": "https://example.edu/iiif/canvas/42r",
  "type": "Canvas",
  "height": 4000,
  "width": 3000,
  "items": [{
    "id": "https://example.edu/iiif/page/42r/1",
    "type": "AnnotationPage",
    "items": [{
      "id": "https://example.edu/iiif/annotation/42r-image",
      "type": "Annotation",
      "motivation": "painting",
      "body": {
        "id": "https://example.edu/iiif/img/42r/full/max/0/default.jpg",
        "type": "Image",
        "format": "image/jpeg",
        "height": 4000,
        "width": 3000
      },
      "target": "https://example.edu/iiif/canvas/42r"
    }]
  }]
}

This is markedly more verbose than simply attaching an image URL to a page, and the verbosity buys something specific. Because association is by annotation, the same mechanism handles every kind of content: a transcription is an annotation with motivation supplementing, a scholarly comment is one with motivation commenting, and a translation is another. One uniform structure covers image, text, and commentary alike.

Version 3.0 adopted the W3C Web Annotation Data Model for this purpose, superseding the earlier Open Annotation model used in 2.1 (IIIF Consortium, 2020). The practical significance is that IIIF annotations are now instances of a general web standard rather than a IIIF-specific invention, and tools built for web annotation work with them.

Takeaway: Content attaches to a canvas by annotation, and because the mechanism is uniform, images, transcriptions, and commentary all attach the same way.

name.text: 09 Content: Presentation API 2.1 and 3.0

questiontext.text:
Presentation API 2.1 and 3.0

You will encounter both versions in the wild, because many institutions still serve 2.1 manifests. The differences matter enough to be worth recognizing on sight (IIIF Consortium, 2020).

Feature Presentation API 2.1 Presentation API 3.0
Annotation model Open Annotation W3C Web Annotation
JSON-LD version 1.0, using @id and @type 1.1, using id and type
Image attachment images array directly on the canvas AnnotationPage holding painting annotations
Labels Plain strings Language maps: {"en": ["..."]}
Audio and video Not supported Native, via duration on the canvas
Layered alternatives No standard mechanism The Choice construct
Supplementary views Modelled ad hoc accompanyingCanvas, placeholderCanvas

The quickest way to identify a manifest's version is the key style. If you see @id and @type, you are reading 2.1; if you see bare id and type, it is 3.0. The @context value states it definitively.

Two of these changes matter directly for your work. The language map for labels means that "label" in 3.0 is always an object keyed by language code containing an array — a shape that trips up everyone writing their first manifest by hand, because a bare string is invalid. And the Choice construct, absent from 2.1, is what makes multi-spectral layering expressible at all; it is the subject of Lesson 3.2 and the reason this course targets 3.0 specifically.

Write 3.0 for your own manifest. Read 2.1 when you must, and be aware that converting between them is not purely mechanical, since 3.0 can express structures 2.1 cannot.

Takeaway: @id means 2.1 and bare id means 3.0; write 3.0, because only it can express layered spectral alternatives.

name.text: 10 Content: The Full Structural Hierarchy

questiontext.text:
The Full Structural Hierarchy

Assembling the pieces, a Presentation 3.0 document has a consistent nesting that is worth committing to memory, since every error message you receive will refer to some level of it.

Level Type Holds Corresponds to
1 Collection Manifests and other collections A library, or a group of manuscripts
2 Manifest Canvases, ranges, metadata One manuscript or one intellectual object
3 Canvas AnnotationPages One page or opening
4 AnnotationPage Annotations A layer of content on the page
5 Annotation A body and a target One assertion: paint this here
6 Body Image, text, or Choice The content being asserted

Alongside canvases, a manifest may carry Ranges in a structures array. Ranges group canvases into meaningful units without changing their order — quires in a codex, books in a work, chapters, or the section of the manuscript your passage occupies. A viewer renders ranges as a table of contents.

This matters for your edition. Your passage is a portion of a manuscript, and a range expresses exactly that relationship: it identifies which canvases constitute your passage while leaving them in place within the manuscript's full sequence. In Week 13, when you publish, this is how a reader will navigate directly to your text within the larger codex.

Two structural rules catch people out. Every canvas must declare height and width, because those define the coordinate space that annotations target and without them targeting is undefined. And every resource needs an id that is a genuine HTTP URI, not an arbitrary local string — the identifiers are meant to be dereferenceable.

Takeaway: Collection, manifest, canvas, annotation page, annotation, body — and ranges group canvases into a table of contents without disturbing their order.

name.text: 11 Content: Case Study: DigitaVaticana and Scale

questiontext.text:
Case Study: DigitaVaticana and Scale

The Vatican Apostolic Library's digitization programme demonstrates what IIIF delivers at scale, and it is the case most directly relevant to your own source selection.

The library holds roughly eighty thousand manuscripts. Digitizing that corpus under the pre-IIIF model would have required pre-generating a full pyramid of static zoom levels for every folio — every resolution, every tile, stored on disk in advance. The storage implications are prohibitive, and the result would be frozen: any change to tile size or zoom behaviour would require regenerating everything.

The IIIF Image API removes the requirement. The library stores one high-resolution master per folio and generates tiles dynamically in response to requests. Storage scales with the number of folios rather than with the number of folios multiplied by zoom levels, and the delivery behaviour can change without touching the stored masters (Griffin, 2023).

On top of that, the Presentation API supplies structure: each codex is described by a manifest carrying its metadata and canvas sequence, served as JSON-LD. Those manifests are consumed by Mirador, an open-source viewer that presents multiple manifests side by side in a single workspace. A scholar can open a Vatican manuscript alongside one from any other IIIF-compliant institution and compare readings at full zoom, without either library having coordinated with the other in any way (Griffin, 2023).

The last clause is the point worth dwelling on. The Vatican did not build an interface for comparing its manuscripts with Leipzig's. It published standard manifests, and comparison became possible as a consequence. That is what a standard does: it makes cooperation happen without requiring coordination.

Takeaway: The Vatican stores one master per folio and generates tiles on demand, and comparison with other libraries works because both publish to the same standard — not because they cooperated.

name.text: 13 Content: Finding IIIF Resources for Your Passage

questiontext.text:
Finding IIIF Resources for Your Passage

You selected a passage in Week 1 and confirmed a IIIF manifest existed. Now locate and record the actual endpoints, because Lesson 3.3 requires them.

Most institutions expose the manifest URL through their viewer interface, though the presentation varies:

  • A "IIIF" logo or drag-and-drop badge, usually near the image — the badge itself is a link to the manifest.
  • A "Share" or "Export" panel offering a manifest URL.
  • A predictable URL pattern, such as https://digi.vatlib.it/iiif/MSS_{shelfmark}/manifest.json.
  • The page source: search the HTML for manifest.json.
  • The browser's network inspector: reload the viewer and look for the JSON request it makes.

The last method always works, because a IIIF viewer cannot function without fetching a manifest. If the other routes fail, open the developer tools, filter network requests for manifest, and reload.

Major repositories with reliable IIIF support include the Vatican Library, the Bibliothèque nationale de France via Gallica, the British Library, e-codices for Swiss manuscripts, the Bodleian's Digital Bodleian, Harvard, Yale's Beinecke, and the Biblissima aggregator. Biblissima is particularly useful for locating witnesses, since it indexes manifests across many institutions.

Record what you find in your repository now — manifest URL, Image API base URL, canvas identifiers for your folios, and the licence and required attribution. A manifest URL that worked in September and was not written down is a genuine obstacle in December.

Takeaway: Every IIIF viewer must fetch a manifest, so the network inspector always reveals the URL when the interface does not.

name.text: 14 Content: Reading a Manifest Critically

questiontext.text:
Reading a Manifest Critically

Having found a manifest, read it rather than merely feeding it to a viewer. It is a scholarly document, and it makes claims you may need to evaluate or dispute.

curl -s https://digi.vatlib.it/iiif/MSS_Vat.gr.1209/manifest.json | python3 -m json.tool | head -60

Interrogate the following:

Question Where to look Why it matters
What version is this? @context Determines what constructs are available
How many canvases? Length of items Confirms the folio range you expected
What are the dimensions? height, width on canvases Determines coordinate precision for Lesson 3.3
What licence applies? rights Governs what you may publish in Week 13
What attribution is required? requiredStatement Must be reproduced in your edition
Is there structure? structures Ranges may already identify your passage
What metadata is asserted? metadata Date and origin claims you may need to assess

The metadata deserves genuine scholarly scepticism. A manifest's assertions about date, origin, and scribe are catalogue claims, sometimes inherited from nineteenth-century descriptions and not always revised since. They are evidence about the manuscript, of the same kind as any other catalogue statement, and they can be wrong. Your Week 2 TEI header records your description, and where it diverges from the manifest's, that divergence is a scholarly claim you should be prepared to defend.

Clausen et al. (2026), arguing for open repositories that integrate manuscript research data, make the related point that descriptive and material data about a manuscript accumulate from many sources and must be kept traceable to those sources rather than merged into an undifferentiated record.

Takeaway: A manifest's metadata is a catalogue claim that can be wrong; read it as evidence, not as fact.

name.text: 15 Content: Rights, Licensing, and What You May Publish

questiontext.text:
Rights, Licensing, and What You May Publish

Because your edition will be published in Week 13, licensing is a practical constraint rather than a formality, and IIIF makes it explicit.

The rights property holds a URI identifying a licence — typically a Creative Commons licence or a RightsStatements.org statement. The requiredStatement holds attribution text that must be displayed wherever the images appear.

Rights value Permits Constraint for Week 13
CC0 Anything, no conditions None
CC BY Reuse with attribution Reproduce the required statement
CC BY-NC Non-commercial reuse only Fine for coursework; limits later reuse
CC BY-SA Reuse if derivatives share the licence Your edition must adopt the same licence
InC (In Copyright) Nothing by default You may link, not reproduce
NoC-NC Non-commercial use; no copyright known Usually workable; read the statement

Two practical rules follow. First, linking is not reproducing. Referencing a canvas URI in your TEI and letting a viewer fetch the image from the institution's server is not republication — the image is served by its owner under its own terms. Copying the image file into your repository is republication, and requires the licence to permit it. Prefer linking; it is both safer and better practice, since the image stays connected to its source.

Second, attribution is not optional and not a matter of politeness. Where requiredStatement is present, displaying it is a licence condition. Build it into your edition's interface rather than adding it at the end.

If your chosen manuscript is In Copyright, raise it this week. It is workable — you link rather than reproduce — but it changes what Week 13 can publish, and that is better known now than in December.

Takeaway: Linking to a canvas is not republication; copying the image file is — so prefer linking, and always display the required attribution.

name.text: 16 Content: JSON-LD: Why the Format Is Not Just JSON

questiontext.text:
JSON-LD: Why the Format Is Not Just JSON

Manifests are JSON-LD, not plain JSON, and the difference is the reason IIIF data composes with other scholarly data.

Plain JSON is machine-readable: a program can parse it into a data structure. But the meaning of its keys is a private convention. A "date" key might hold a manuscript's date of production, its date of digitization, or the date the record was edited, and nothing in the JSON says which. A program must be told, by a human, what the publisher meant.

JSON-LD adds a @context that maps keys to URIs in shared vocabularies (IIIF Consortium, 2020). Once "label" is defined as a specific term in the IIIF vocabulary, its meaning is stated in the data rather than assumed. The document becomes machine-interpretable: a program that has never encountered this institution's manifests can still determine what each field asserts.

This makes manifests Linked Data — part of a graph in which resources are identified by URIs and can be referenced from outside. The consequence for scholarship is that a manuscript's canvas can be cited from anywhere: your TEI transcription in Lesson 3.3 will reference a Vatican canvas URI directly, and that reference is meaningful to any system that understands the vocabulary.

The connection to Week 2 is direct. The RDF triples you built for your TEI header and IIIF's JSON-LD are two serializations of the same underlying model — subject, predicate, object, with URIs as identifiers. Your metadata and your images are already in the same graph, which is what will let Week 13 publish them as a single connected resource.

Vocabulary. Linked Data — data published with URI identifiers and shared vocabularies so that it can be referenced and combined across sources. @context — the JSON-LD element mapping keys to vocabulary URIs.

Takeaway: JSON-LD states the meaning of its keys in the data, which is what lets a manifest be cited from and combined with other scholarly data.

name.text: 17 Content: Canvas Coordinates and Fragment Selectors

questiontext.text:
Canvas Coordinates and Fragment Selectors

Since a canvas is a coordinate space, any region of it can be addressed precisely. The mechanism is the fragment selector, appended to a canvas URI with #:

https://example.edu/iiif/canvas/42r#xywh=1200,400,800,600

The xywh selector names four integers: the x and y coordinates of the region's top-left corner, then its width and height, all in canvas coordinate units. Coordinates originate at the top-left of the canvas, with x increasing rightwards and y increasing downwards — the standard convention in computer graphics, and the opposite of mathematical convention on the y axis, which catches people out.

Selector Addresses
#xywh=0,0,3000,4000 The entire canvas, if it is 3000 by 4000
#xywh=1200,400,800,600 An 800 by 600 region at (1200, 400)
#xywh=pct:25,10,50,15 A percentage-based region, resolution-independent

The percentage form deserves attention. Absolute pixel coordinates are tied to a particular canvas size; if the manifest is ever regenerated from a rescanned master at different dimensions, every absolute coordinate silently becomes wrong. Percentage coordinates survive that change. For a course edition the absolute form is generally acceptable and is what most tools emit, but record the canvas dimensions alongside your coordinates so that the values can be recomputed if needed.

This is the mechanism that binds text to image, and it is the crux of Lesson 3.3. A line of your transcription will carry a @facs attribute pointing at exactly the region of the canvas that shows it — so that a reader clicking a word is taken to the parchment.

Takeaway: #xywh=x,y,w,h addresses any rectangle of a canvas, and this is the mechanism that will bind your transcription to the image.

name.text: 18 Content: Palaeography and the Digital Surrogate

questiontext.text:
Palaeography and the Digital Surrogate

A methodological question arises before the technical work goes further. What is the epistemological status of the digital image relative to the manuscript?

The traditional answer was that the surrogate is a degraded substitute: photography loses information — colour fidelity, surface texture, the physical sense of the object — and serious palaeographical judgement therefore requires autopsy, direct inspection of the original. On that view digitization is a convenience for preliminary work, with real conclusions reserved for the manuscript itself.

That answer is now only partly right, and the qualification is the point of this week. In some respects the surrogate remains poorer: no photograph conveys the weight and drape of a codex, and colour is never fully faithful. In other respects the surrogate is better than autopsy — it can be magnified beyond what the eye resolves, illuminated in wavelengths the eye cannot see, and processed to separate signals the eye cannot distinguish (Easton et al., 2003).

Griffin (2023), surveying digital infrastructures for epigraphy and palaeography, describes this as a genuine shift in what these disciplines can investigate, rather than as improved access to unchanged objects. The digital surrogate is not a photograph of the manuscript; it is a dataset derived from it, and its relation to the original is more like that of a scientific instrument's output than of a picture.

The practical corollary matters for your own claims. When you assert a reading this term, you should be able to say what evidence supports it and under what conditions that evidence was produced — which image, which wavelength, which processing. Lesson 3.2 concerns exactly those conditions, and Lesson 3.3 concerns recording them.

Takeaway: A digital surrogate is a dataset derived from the manuscript, not a picture of it, and in some respects it shows more than autopsy can.

name.text: 19 Content: Case Study: Codex Sinaiticus and Virtual Reunification

questiontext.text:
Case Study: Codex Sinaiticus and Virtual Reunification

Sinaiticus makes the interoperability argument concrete, and it is worth following the case through.

Written in the fourth century, it is among the oldest substantially complete manuscripts of the Christian Bible and a witness of the first importance for the text of both Testaments. In the nineteenth century its leaves were dispersed, and they now rest in four institutions: the British Library, Leipzig University Library, St Catherine's Monastery in Sinai, and the National Library of Russia.

The scholarly consequence was severe. The manuscript is one object and one scribal undertaking, but no scholar could examine it as such. Study meant travelling between four institutions across three continents, or relying on photographic facsimiles that fixed a single interpretation of each page and could not be re-examined under different conditions.

Digitization with interoperable delivery permits virtual reunification: the dispersed leaves are described by manifests, and a viewer assembles them into their original sequence regardless of where each is physically held. Imaging that enhanced the faded carbon inks additionally revealed textual variants and scribal corrections that had not been legible in earlier facsimiles.

Note the double gain, because it recurs throughout the week. Interoperability solved a distribution problem — the leaves could be brought together. Imaging solved a legibility problem — the text could be read. Neither addresses the other, and both were needed. Lesson 3.2 takes up the second.

Takeaway: Sinaiticus needed two distinct advances — interoperability to reunite dispersed leaves, and enhanced imaging to make the ink legible.

name.text: 20 Content: Validating a Manifest

questiontext.text:
Validating a Manifest

Manifests you write by hand will contain errors, and a viewer's response to an invalid manifest is usually to display nothing with no explanation. Validate deliberately.

Check Tool Catches
Well-formed JSON python3 -m json.tool Trailing commas, unclosed brackets, bad quoting
IIIF conformance The IIIF Presentation Validator Missing required properties; wrong types
Renders correctly Load into Mirador Structural problems the validator permits
Images resolve curl -I on each image URI Broken or moved image endpoints

Run them in that order, since each presupposes the previous. Malformed JSON cannot be checked for conformance; a non-conformant manifest will not render; a manifest that renders may still point at images that have moved.

The errors that recur most often when writing 3.0 by hand:

  • A label given as a plain string instead of a language map — "label": "f. 42r" rather than "label": {"en": ["f. 42r"]}.
  • A canvas without height and width, leaving the coordinate space undefined.
  • Images attached directly to the canvas in the 2.1 style, instead of through an AnnotationPage.
  • An id that is not an HTTP URI.
  • A target naming a canvas id that does not exist, usually a typo.

Add validation to your pre-commit hook, exactly as you did for XML in Week 1. A malformed manifest committed on a Tuesday and discovered on a Friday is an avoidable loss.

Takeaway: Validate as JSON, then for IIIF conformance, then by rendering, then by checking that the images actually resolve.

name.text: 21 Content: Level 0 and Level 2 Image Services

questiontext.text:
Level 0 and Level 2 Image Services

Not every IIIF image server offers the same capabilities, and the difference will affect what you can do with a given source. The Image API defines compliance levels.

Level Supports Typical implementation
Level 0 Only pre-generated static sizes and regions Static files on ordinary web hosting
Level 1 Region and size requests; limited transformation Lightweight servers
Level 2 Arbitrary regions, sizes, rotation, quality, formats Full image servers: Cantaloupe, IIPImage, Loris

The distinction becomes concrete in Week 13. A Level 2 service permits any region at any size on demand, which is what dynamic deep zoom requires. A Level 0 service serves only the derivatives that were generated in advance — a request for an arbitrary region simply fails.

The reason this matters to you is that Level 0 is often the practical option for publishing your own images. Running Cantaloupe requires a server you administer; generating a fixed tile pyramid and serving it as static files requires only web hosting, and works on GitHub Pages. If in Week 13 you publish your own derived images — a processed composite, for instance — you will most likely produce a Level 0 service with a tool such as iiif_static.py.

The manifest declares the level in each image body's service block, so you can determine in advance what a source supports. If you plan to extract arbitrary regions from an institution's images for your commentary, confirm Level 2 before depending on it.

Takeaway: Level 2 serves arbitrary regions on demand; Level 0 serves only pre-generated derivatives, and is what static hosting supports.

name.text: 22 Content: Content Search and Navigation APIs

questiontext.text:
Content Search and Navigation APIs

Two further IIIF specifications are worth knowing, because they become relevant to your published edition in Week 13.

The Content Search API defines a standard way to search annotations attached to a manifest and to receive results with their canvas coordinates. Where a transcription has been attached as annotations, a viewer implementing Content Search lets a reader search the text and be taken to the corresponding place on the image. For a digital edition this is the capability that makes the transcription usable rather than merely present.

The Change Discovery API publishes a stream of changes to a collection, so that aggregators can learn when manifests are added or updated without polling. This is what allows services like Biblissima to index manifests across dozens of institutions and keep the index current.

API Purpose Relevance to your edition
Image Deliver image regions Every week from now on
Presentation Describe structure Lesson 3.3
Content Search Search annotations, return coordinates Week 13 publication
Change Discovery Announce updates to a collection Aggregation; contextual
Authentication Control access to restricted images Only if your source is restricted

You are not required to implement Content Search this term. It is worth knowing that the capability is standardized, because it shapes what you should aim at: if your transcription is bound to canvas coordinates — which is precisely what Lesson 3.3 does — then a searchable image-linked edition is a matter of configuration rather than of redesign.

Takeaway: Binding your transcription to canvas coordinates now is what makes a searchable, image-linked edition possible later.

The Week 4 dependency is the most immediate. An apparatus entry recording a variant reading can carry the canvas region showing that reading in each witness — so that a reader evaluating your editorial decision sees the parchment rather than taking your word for it. name.text: 24 Content: The Multimodal Repository Argument

questiontext.text:
The Multimodal Repository Argument

Clausen et al. (2026) extend the interoperability argument beyond images, and their framing is useful for understanding where this is all heading.

Their observation is that a manuscript under modern investigation generates many kinds of data. Multispectral imaging produces datacubes. X-ray fluorescence produces elemental maps. Raman spectroscopy characterizes pigments. Codicological examination produces structural description. Transcription produces TEI. Each has traditionally been held by the discipline that produced it, in its own format, in its own repository — and the connections between them, which are where the interesting questions live, are lost.

Their proposal is an open repository integrating these heterogeneous datasets around the physical object, linking material analyses to structural textual encodings so that a question spanning them can be asked at all (Clausen et al., 2026).

Data type Produced by Traditionally held in
Multispectral datacube Imaging science Imaging lab archives
XRF elemental map Conservation science Conservation records
Raman pigment analysis Materials chemistry Chemistry publications
Codicological description Manuscript studies Library catalogues
Transcription and apparatus Textual criticism Editions and TEI repositories

IIIF is a substantial part of the answer, because the canvas provides a shared coordinate space that every one of these can target. An elemental map, a processed composite, and a transcribed line can all address the same region of the same canvas — which is exactly what makes them relatable.

Your own edition is a small instance of this. By Week 13 it will link codicological description, images under multiple conditions, transcription, apparatus, and commentary, all anchored to a common coordinate space.

Takeaway: The canvas is a shared coordinate space that imaging, materials analysis, and transcription can all target, which is what makes them relatable.

name.text: 25 Content: Persistent Identifiers and Citation

questiontext.text:
Persistent Identifiers and Citation

An edition that cannot be cited stably is not scholarship, and IIIF resources are identified by URIs — which are notoriously unstable.

The problem is real. Institutions reorganize, domains lapse, platforms migrate, and a canvas URI cited in a 2026 article may resolve to nothing in 2036. This is the digital equivalent of a shelfmark changing after a library recatalogues, with the difference that the digital failure is silent and total.

Mitigations, in order of reliability:

Approach Mechanism Durability
DOI Registered persistent identifier with maintained resolution High; the scholarly standard
ARK Archival Resource Key, widely used by libraries High where the institution maintains it
Purl Redirection service under the publisher's control Moderate
Institutional URI The library's own URL scheme Variable; depends on institutional stability
Ad-hoc URL Whatever the current platform emits Low

For your own citations this term, record the DOI or ARK where one exists, and the full canvas URI in every case. Where a manifest carries a seeAlso block, follow it — institutions frequently link the persistent catalogue record there.

Also record what you saw and when. A citation of the form "MS Vat. gr. 1209, f. 42r, canvas https://…/canvas/p42, accessed 15 September 2026, image dimensions 3000×4000" survives partial link rot: even if the URI stops resolving, a reader can identify the folio and the exact region you meant. Your Week 1 commit discipline is the mechanism here — record the identifiers in the repository, at the time you use them.

Takeaway: Record DOIs, full canvas URIs, dimensions, and access dates, so that your citations survive the link rot that will eventually occur.

questiontext.text:
A Practical Exercise for This Meeting

Work through the following now, on your own passage. Everything in Lesson 3.3 assumes it is complete.

  • Locate the manifest URL for your primary witness and record it in your repository.
  • Retrieve it with curl and pretty-print it; do not merely open it in a viewer.
  • Identify the canvases corresponding to your folios and record their ids.
  • Record each canvas's height and width.
  • Extract the rights value and the requiredStatement.
  • Construct an Image API URL by hand that returns the full folio at 1000 pixels wide, and open it.
  • Construct a second that returns only the region containing the first line of your passage.
  • Load the manifest into Mirador and confirm it renders.
  • Repeat for your second witness.
  • Commit all of it as a structured note in your repository.

The hand-constructed URLs matter more than they appear. Anyone can drag a manifest into a viewer; being able to write an Image API request from scratch is what lets you extract precisely the evidence you need, script it over many folios, and diagnose failures when a viewer shows nothing.

Record the results as a Markdown file in your repository — images/SOURCES.md is a reasonable location — and commit it with a Conventional Commits message. In Week 13 this file is the basis of your edition's image documentation.

Takeaway: Write the Image API URLs by hand; that skill is what makes you independent of any particular viewer.

name.text: 27 Content: Common Failures and Their Diagnosis

questiontext.text:
Common Failures and Their Diagnosis

Predictable failures, so you recognize them rather than rediscovering them.

Symptom Likely cause Diagnosis
Viewer shows nothing, no error Invalid manifest Run the IIIF validator
Manifest loads, images blank Image endpoints moved or restricted curl -I each image URI
Images load in one viewer, not another Version mismatch, 2.1 versus 3.0 Inspect @context
Cross-origin error in the browser console Server lacks CORS headers Check response headers; contact the institution
Zoom stops at low magnification Level 0 service; no higher tiles exist Inspect the service block
Coordinates address the wrong region Canvas dimensions differ from image dimensions Compare canvas height/width with the image
Labels display as [object Object] Language map handled as a string, or vice versa Check the label's shape against the version

The CORS case is worth explaining, since it produces the most bewildering symptom. A browser refuses to let a page fetch data from another domain unless that domain's server explicitly permits it with a Cross-Origin Resource Sharing header. If an institution's server omits the header, its manifest works in that institution's own viewer and fails everywhere else — an accidental silo, reproducing the exact problem IIIF was built to eliminate. Nothing on your side can fix it; the remedy is to report it to the institution, which usually treats it as the bug it is.

The last row is the classic hand-authoring error and the one most likely to bite you on Friday. In 2.1 a label is a string; in 3.0 it is a language map holding arrays. Mixing them produces exactly this symptom.

Takeaway: Diagnose in order — validate the manifest, check the image endpoints, then check the version — and recognize CORS failures as the institution's bug, not yours.

name.text: 28 Content: What a Canvas Is Not

questiontext.text:
What a Canvas Is Not

A consolidating exercise, since the canvas abstraction is where conceptual errors concentrate and each error has a characteristic downstream symptom.

Misconception Why it is wrong Consequence
"A canvas is an image" It is a coordinate space; images are painted onto it Cannot model multispectral layers
"A canvas has one image" It may carry many, including alternatives Cannot model a Choice
"Canvas dimensions are image dimensions" They may differ; images are scaled to fit Coordinates address the wrong region
"A canvas must have an image" An empty canvas can represent a lost folio Cannot model lacunae in a codex
"A canvas is a page" It is an abstraction that usually stands for a page Cannot model an opening, a fragment, or a reconstruction

The third row causes the most practical trouble and is worth stating carefully. Canvas dimensions define the coordinate space, and images are painted into that space — scaled if their pixel dimensions differ. If a canvas is 3000×4000 while the image is 6000×8000, then canvas coordinate (1500, 2000) corresponds to image pixel (3000, 4000). Fragment selectors address canvas coordinates. Computing a region from the image's pixel dimensions when the canvas differs puts your annotation in the wrong place, and the error is systematic rather than random — everything is off by the same factor, which makes it easy to miss and easy to correct once seen.

Always read the canvas dimensions from the manifest, and never assume they match the image.

Takeaway: Fragment selectors address canvas coordinates, not image pixels, and the two frequently differ by a scale factor.

name.text: 29 Content: Preparing for Lesson 3.2

questiontext.text:
Preparing for Lesson 3.2

Wednesday moves from delivery to acquisition — from how images are served to how they are made, and to what can be recovered from a manuscript that ordinary photography cannot show.

The connection is the canvas abstraction established today. Multispectral imaging produces many images of one folio: visible light, ultraviolet, several infrared bands, and statistically processed composites. In a model where a page has one image, these are unrelated files that a scholar must manage by hand. In the IIIF model they are alternative content painted onto a single canvas, and a viewer can present them as toggleable layers over one coordinate space.

That is why this week is ordered as it is. The Choice construct introduced tomorrow is meaningless without today's understanding that a canvas is a space rather than a picture, and the coordinate binding on Friday is meaningless without both.

Before Wednesday:

  • Complete the exercise in section 26 for both witnesses.
  • Confirm Mirador renders both manifests.
  • Note whether either institution provides non-visible-light images — search the manifest for terms such as ultraviolet, infrared, UV, IR, or processed.
  • Read the rights statements and record what they permit.

The third item is genuinely worth doing. Multispectral captures exist for many manuscripts but are frequently not surfaced in the default viewer, appearing only as additional entries in the manifest. If your manuscript has them, Wednesday's work applies directly to your own edition rather than to an example.

Takeaway: The canvas-as-space abstraction is what makes tomorrow's spectral layering expressible; check now whether your own manuscript has non-visible-light captures.

name.text: 30 Content: Synthesis: Images as Addressable Scholarly Resources

questiontext.text:
Synthesis: Images as Addressable Scholarly Resources

The argument of this meeting, stated once more in its own terms.

Digitization alone produced silos. Millions of manuscript images existed, each accessible only through the interface of the institution that made it, which meant that the fundamental operation of textual criticism — juxtaposing witnesses — remained obstructed. The obstruction was not technical scarcity but the absence of a shared standard.

IIIF resolves it by making images addressable. The Image API gives every region of every image a URL constructed by a rule anyone can apply. The Presentation API describes objects in a shared vocabulary, so that any viewer can render any institution's manifest. Cooperation happens without coordination, because both parties implement the same specification (Griffin, 2023; IIIF Consortium, 2020).

The abstraction that carries the most weight is the canvas: a coordinate space standing for the page, onto which evidence is painted. This is what permits many images of one page, transcriptions bound to regions of it, annotations targeting its coordinates, and the whole multimodal integration that Clausen et al. (2026) argue manuscript scholarship now requires.

For Wednesday. Complete the section 26 exercise for both witnesses, confirm both render in Mirador, and check your manifests for non-visible-light captures.

For Friday. The Cataloguing & Metadata Assignment is due Friday September 18, and Friday's meeting builds the manifest for your passage and binds it to your TEI. Everything recorded today is the input to that work.

Takeaway: IIIF makes every region of every image addressable by a shared rule, and the canvas — a coordinate space, not a picture — is what lets images, text, and analysis all refer to the same place.
